definition: Indomitable means impossible to defeat or discourage.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word indomitable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know indomitable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Losing her sight at fifty slowed Judge Rivera for exactly one season; the indomitable jurist learned braille within the year and never missed another term of court.
A persistent salesman calls back twice; indomitable belongs to people whom no string of failures can discourage at all.
Tenacious grips hard and refuses to let go, but even tenacity can be worn down; indomitable says the spirit cannot be broken, period.

Unconquerable says no outside force can defeat you - the fortress, the army, the champion team. Indomitable moves the claim inside: a spirit that defeat cannot discourage, whatever the scoreboard says. An unconquerable team never loses; an indomitable one can lose repeatedly and come back undiminished.

Invincible means unbeatable in the contest itself - the champion no rival can touch. Indomitable makes no promise about winning: it describes the will, not the record. Invincible people never taste defeat; indomitable people taste it and refuse to let it discourage them.

Unstoppable describes motion and momentum - once something is moving, nothing halts it. Indomitable is about what happens after a stop: knocked down, turned away, rejected, the indomitable spirit simply cannot be discouraged. Unstoppable never meets the wall; indomitable hits it and comes back.

A hand injury ended cellist Ana Marin's concert career at thirty.
She retrained as a conductor, was turned away from two academies for lacking experience, founded her own chamber orchestra instead, and sold out its first season.
Critics who once pitied her now reach for one word: indomitable.
Indomitable is built on 'cannot be tamed': it describes a spirit that defeat cannot break and discouragement cannot reach.
Tireless people keep working; indomitable people keep coming back.
Indomitable is the strongest refusal-to-quit word in this unit and always admiring.
Resolute praises firmness about a decision; assiduous praises unflagging care; indomitable goes further than either, claiming that no defeat can discourage the person at all.
Save it for spirits, wills, and characters - not for mild stubbornness.

Frankie Owens first tried to swim the strait at nineteen and was pulled out, shaking, two miles short.
She tried again at twenty-one and met a bloom of jellyfish; at twenty-three, a storm turned her back within sight of the far shore.
The harbor crowd stopped debating whether she would ever finish and started marveling at something else: three failures had not dimmed her by a single degree.
Reporters who met her at the dock called the swimmer indomitable, because each defeat seemed only to fix her next departure date.
At twenty-six she finally touched the far rocks, but those who knew her insisted the crossing proved nothing the failed attempts had not already shown.
